newsitem.title: PERU: Peru VIP hostages prepare for gloomy Christmas Eve.
newsitem.headline: Peru VIP hostages prepare for gloomy Christmas Eve.

text.p: More than 140 VIP hostages prepared for a miserable Christmas Eve in Lima on Tuesday as captives of defiant Marxist rebels in the seventh day of a showdown with the Peruvian government.

The men received Christmas cakes from the Red Cross, but had little else to cheer them as they faced the festive holiday under the guns of 20 heavily-armed guerrillas from the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) instead of with their familes.

Red Cross spokesman Steve Andersen told reporters that aid workers would send in "something special" on Tuesday for the men inside the Japanese ambassador's residence, which the MRTA seized during a cocktail party last Tuesday.
Latin Americans traditionally celebrate Christmas with a family meal on the night of December 24.
Following the release on Sunday night of 225 hostages as a "Christmas gesture," the guerrillas in Lima maintained an ominous silence.
In Hamburg, Germany, however, a man claiming to be their international spokesman said the MRTA would never surrender.

"Effectively, what the government of President (Albert) Fujimori is asking is that the group ... gives up," said Isaac Velzaco in a television interview with Cable News Network. "The word surrender or capitulation is not in the vocabulary of the Tupac Amaru soldier."
Earlier on Monday, a woman claiming to be Velazco's wife, Norma Velazco, called a Paraguayan radio station from Hamburg claiming the MRTA was planning more attacks.

Police sources in Lima concurred, telling Reuters they believed another clandestine MRTA commando unit was at large in the Peruvian capital and could strike if dialogue breaks down. "If (police) storm the embassy, it is possible they will start car bomb attacks or other sabotage," one source said.

On the government side, a Peruvian crack commando team was standing by to storm the residence as a last resort if necessary. However, Fujimori, in his only words to the public since the siege began, told the rebels he would not use force and would consider a peaceful "way out" if they laid down their arms and gave up all their hostages.
His plea, and later ones from from U.S. President Bill Clinton and Pope John Paul to release the captives, seems to have fallen on deaf ears.
The government kept electricity, water and telephone services to the building cut on Tuesday.
Unlike previous days, no new signs with messages were thrust up to windows of the residence on Monday, and Red Cross officials said no negotiator had been in since Sunday.
The MRTA's seized the residence last Tuesday during a smart reception to commemorate Japanese Emperor Akihito's birthday, taking more than 500 hostages.
Most -- including all the American, British and German captives -- have now been freed.
But the rebels were still holding at gunpoint dozens of top Peruvian governnment officials and about 30 high-ranking Japanese businessmen and diplomats.

The Red Cross was trying to establish the identity of seven of the 225 freed on Sunday night whose names did not match those on a master list of captives to be freed. It was not clear whether the seven had deliberately used false names or whether the confusion was simply an administrative glitch.
One theory was that an MRTA rebel might have slipped out.
Remaining captives in the residence -- and waiting hordes of journalists from around the world -- could face a long stay.

The rebels, led by Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, a textile worker turned revolutionary, have demanded that the government set free jailed MRTA comrades before ending the siege, but Fujimori has flatly refused.

The president and his interior minister, Gen. Juan Briones Davila, paid a brief first visit on Monday to the scene of the siege but did not get out of their bullet-proofed cars or make any comment before driving off, witnesses said.

Reflecting the grief felt in Japan, Emperor Akihito cancelled all official birthday celebrations on Monday, and Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto tracked the crisis from a special war room in the Foreign Ministry fitted out with television monitors.
"I think it will take time (to resolve the crisis)," Hashimoto told reporters on Tuesday shortly after speaking by telephone with Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori.
Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda called off a visit to South Korea on Tuesday and said "difficult judgments" were now needed to resolve the crisis in Peru.
As families of the released hostages celebrated in Lima, Clinton welcomed the freeing of all seven American captives and called for the immediate release of those still held.

Most Peruvians, long tired of rebel violence, have backed Fujimori's hard line against the rebels. But released hostages said on Monday the lack of water in the residence was endangering the health and safety of those still inside.
"It is extremely important that water is restored," released hostage Victor Lucero told local television. "Water is indispensable. Without it the situation is very dangerous."
Lucero, a doctor, said captives had developed at least eight cases of an eye infection because of the unhygienic conditions. Outbreaks of diarrhoea have also been reported.

The heavily armed young rebels have booby-trapped the entrances of the building and carry backpacks full of explosives. Police say the guerrillas include four sharpshooters at strategic windows armed with telescopic night-sight rifles.
About 900 policemen surrounded the residence on Tuesday, the same number as throughout the crisis.
Salads, chicken and desserts were taken in to feed the captives, and reporters waiting outside behind police lines put up Christmas trees and decorations.

Though police describe MRTA leader Cerpa as a "vicious terrorist" with a long history of bloody attacks, the rebels appear to have treated their captives well and tried to present an image as concerned social crusaders.
